subject: chemistry
title: Molecular shape
summary: Uses VSEPR theory to predict shapes and bond angles for two to six electron domains, including trigonal bipyramidal, see-saw, T-shaped, octahedral, square pyramidal and square planar molecules, and explains molecular polarity and dipole moments.
body:
The three-dimensional shape of a molecule decides how it behaves: whether it is polar, how strongly its molecules attract each other, what it dissolves in, and how it fits into an enzyme or a receptor. **Valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) theory** predicts shape from a Lewis structure with one simple idea. This lesson extends VCE VSEPR to five and six electron domains, explains how lone pairs distort bond angles, and uses bond dipoles to decide whether a molecule has a dipole moment.

## Think of it like this

### Electron domain geometry versus shape is like a group photo with invisible friends

Imagine taking a group photo where some of your friends are invisible. They still take up space, so everyone else has to stand around them, but the photo only shows the visible people. The **electron domain geometry** is the arrangement of everyone in the group, including the invisible friends (the **lone pairs**). The **molecular geometry** — the shape you name — is just what shows up in the photo: the positions of the atoms. That is why NH₃ has a tetrahedral electron domain geometry but a trigonal pyramidal shape, and H₂O is bent.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* lone pairs are not hidden atoms — they are regions of electron density on the central atom, and they actually take up *more* room than a bonding pair, which an ordinary invisible friend would not.

### A lone pair is like a passenger with a huge backpack on the tram

On a crowded tram, someone wearing a big backpack takes up more room than everyone else and pushes the people next to them closer together. A lone pair does the same: it is held by only one nucleus, so it spreads out near the central atom and squeezes the bonding pairs together. This is why the repulsion order is **lone pair–lone pair greater than lone pair–bonding pair greater than bonding pair–bonding pair**, and why the bond angles fall from 109.5° in CH₄ to 107° in NH₃ and 104.5° in H₂O. In a **trigonal bipyramid**, the backpack passenger heads for an **equatorial** spot, which has fewer neighbours pressed up against them at 90°.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* the tram passenger chooses where to stand, but the molecule simply adopts whichever arrangement has the lowest energy — and VSEPR only predicts the general pattern, so exact angles like 173° in SF₄ come from experiment.

### In real life

The shape of a molecule decides how it fits into an enzyme or a receptor in your body, which is why many medicines work only if they have exactly the right 3D shape. Shape also decides polarity: water's bent shape makes it polar, which is why it can dissolve table salt and sugar, while the carbon dioxide that makes soft drinks fizzy is non-polar even though its C=O bonds are polar, because its linear shape makes the bond dipoles cancel.

## Key ideas

### The VSEPR idea

Electron pairs in the valence shell of a central atom repel one another and arrange themselves as far apart as possible. Each region of electron density around the central atom is an **electron domain**. A domain can be a single bond, a double bond, a triple bond (each counts as one domain) or a lone pair. Two arrangements must be kept separate:

- The **electron domain geometry** is the arrangement of all domains, bonding and non-bonding.
- The **molecular geometry** (the shape) describes only the positions of the atoms. Lone pairs affect the shape but are not "seen" in it.

The method is: draw the Lewis structure, count domains on the central atom, find the electron domain geometry, then name the shape from the positions of the atoms. The notation **AXₘEₙ** is useful: A is the central atom, X a bonded atom and E a lone pair.

### Strength of repulsions

Not all domains repel equally. A lone pair is held by only one nucleus, so it spreads out closer to the central atom and takes up more room than a bonding pair. The order of repulsion is:

`lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair`

Multiple bonds also take up a little more room than single bonds. This explains why the H–N–H angle in NH₃ (107°) and the H–O–H angle in H₂O (104.5°) are smaller than the ideal tetrahedral 109.5°.

### Two, three and four domains

| Domains | Electron domain geometry | AXₘEₙ | Shape | Ideal angle | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | linear | AX₂ | linear | 180° | CO₂, BeCl₂ |
| 3 | trigonal planar | AX₃ | trigonal planar | 120° | BF₃, SO₃ |
| 3 | trigonal planar | AX₂E | bent | < 120° | SO₂ (about 119°) |
| 4 | tetrahedral | AX₄ | tetrahedral | 109.5° | CH₄ |
| 4 | tetrahedral | AX₃E | trigonal pyramidal | < 109.5° | NH₃ (107°) |
| 4 | tetrahedral | AX₂E₂ | bent | < 109.5° | H₂O (104.5°) |

### Five domains: trigonal bipyramidal family

Five domains (for central atoms in period 3 or below, with expanded octets) form a **trigonal bipyramid**. Its positions are not all the same:

- three **equatorial** positions in a triangle around the "waist", 120° apart;
- two **axial** positions above and below, at 90° to the equatorial plane and 180° to each other.

An axial position has three neighbours at 90°; an equatorial position has only two neighbours at 90°. Since repulsion at 90° is far stronger than at 120°, **lone pairs always go in equatorial positions first**, where they have fewer close neighbours.

| AXₘEₙ | Shape | Angles | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| AX₅ | trigonal bipyramidal | 90°, 120°, 180° | PCl₅ |
| AX₄E | see-saw | < 90°, < 120° | SF₄ |
| AX₃E₂ | T-shaped | < 90° | ClF₃ |
| AX₂E₃ | linear | 180° | XeF₂, I₃⁻ |

In XeF₂, the three lone pairs occupy all three equatorial positions, leaving the two F atoms axial, so the molecule is exactly linear. In SF₄ the single lone pair compresses the remaining angles, so the axial F–S–F angle is about 173° (not 180°) and the equatorial angle about 102° (not 120°).

### Six domains: octahedral family

Six domains form an **octahedron**. All six positions are equivalent, with 90° between neighbours and 180° between opposite positions.

| AXₘEₙ | Shape | Angles | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| AX₆ | octahedral | 90°, 180° | SF₆ |
| AX₅E | square pyramidal | < 90° | BrF₅, IF₅ |
| AX₄E₂ | square planar | 90°, 180° | XeF₄, ICl₄⁻ |

The first lone pair can go anywhere. A second lone pair goes **opposite** the first (trans, 180° apart), not next to it, to avoid a lone pair–lone pair interaction at 90°. That is why AX₄E₂ is square planar.

### Molecular polarity and dipole moments

A polar bond has a **bond dipole**, a vector pointing from the δ+ atom towards the δ− atom. The **dipole moment**, μ, measures the separation of charge: μ = Q × r, where Q is the size of the separated charge and r the distance between the charges. It is measured in **debye** (D), where 1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m.

The overall dipole moment of a molecule is the **vector sum** of its bond dipoles (lone pairs also contribute). So polarity depends on both bond polarity and shape:

- A molecule with no polar bonds is non-polar.
- A molecule with polar bonds arranged **symmetrically**, so the bond dipoles cancel, is non-polar (μ = 0). Examples: CO₂ (linear), BF₃ (trigonal planar), CCl₄ (tetrahedral), PCl₅, SF₆, XeF₄ (square planar) and XeF₂ (linear).
- A molecule with polar bonds that do not cancel is polar (μ > 0). Examples: H₂O (1.85 D), NH₃ (1.47 D), SO₂, SF₄, ClF₃ and BrF₅.

A useful check: if all the outer positions of a perfectly symmetric shape (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral, square planar) are the same atom, the molecule is non-polar. Replacing even one atom with a different one usually makes it polar: CH₄ is non-polar, but CH₃Cl is polar.

Polarity matters because polar molecules attract each other through dipole–dipole forces, which raises boiling points, and because "like dissolves like": polar solutes tend to dissolve in polar solvents.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: the shape of SF₄

1. Valence electrons: S = 6, F = 4 × 7 = 28. Total = 34.
2. Four S–F single bonds use 8 electrons. Each F needs 3 lone pairs: 12 pairs = 24 electrons. Used so far: 32.
3. Remaining 2 electrons form one lone pair on S.
4. Domains on S: 4 bonding + 1 lone = 5, so the electron domain geometry is trigonal bipyramidal (AX₄E).
5. The lone pair goes equatorial, so the shape is **see-saw**, with angles a little less than 90° and 120°.
6. The S–F bond dipoles do not cancel in this unsymmetrical shape, so SF₄ is **polar**.

### Example 2: the shape of XeF₄

1. Valence electrons: Xe = 8, F = 4 × 7 = 28. Total = 36.
2. Four Xe–F bonds (8) plus 3 lone pairs on each F (24) = 32 electrons used.
3. Remaining 4 electrons form 2 lone pairs on Xe.
4. Domains: 4 bonding + 2 lone = 6, so octahedral electron domain geometry (AX₄E₂).
5. The two lone pairs sit opposite each other, so the shape is **square planar**, with F–Xe–F angles of 90° and 180°.
6. The four Xe–F bond dipoles point to the corners of a square and cancel, so XeF₄ is **non-polar** despite having polar bonds.

### Example 3: the triiodide ion, I₃⁻

1. Valence electrons: 3 × 7 + 1 = 22.
2. Two I–I bonds (4) and 3 lone pairs on each end I (12) use 16. Remaining 6 electrons form 3 lone pairs on the central I.
3. Domains: 2 bonding + 3 lone = 5, trigonal bipyramidal (AX₂E₃).
4. All three lone pairs go equatorial, so the ion is **linear** (180°).

### Example 4: estimating a partial charge from a dipole moment

HCl has μ = 1.08 D and bond length 127 pm. Estimate the partial charge on each atom as a fraction of the electron charge (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C).

1. Convert μ: 1.08 D × 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m D⁻¹ = 3.603 × 10⁻³⁰ C m.
2. Rearrange μ = Q × r: Q = μ/r = (3.603 × 10⁻³⁰ C m) / (1.27 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) = 2.837 × 10⁻²⁰ C.
3. As a fraction of e: 2.837 × 10⁻²⁰ / 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ = **0.177**.

So H carries about +0.18 and Cl about −0.18. The bond is about 18% ionic in character: clearly polar, but far from fully ionic.

## Common mistakes

- Naming the electron domain geometry instead of the shape. NH₃ has tetrahedral electron domain geometry but a trigonal pyramidal shape.
- Putting lone pairs in axial positions in five-domain molecules. Lone pairs go equatorial, which is what makes XeF₂ linear and ClF₃ T-shaped.
- Putting the two lone pairs of AX₄E₂ next to each other. They go opposite, giving square planar, not see-saw.
- Assuming any molecule with polar bonds is polar. Symmetric shapes such as CCl₄, XeF₄ and SF₆ have μ = 0.
- Forgetting to count lone pairs on the central atom after completing outer-atom octets, especially for xenon and halogen compounds.

## Exam tips

- Always show the Lewis structure, the domain count and the AXₘEₙ label before naming the shape; method marks are given for each step.
- When asked for bond angles, give the ideal angle and say whether lone pairs make it smaller (for example "less than 109.5°, about 107°").
- For polarity questions, state bond polarity (with electronegativities if needed) and then whether the shape lets the dipoles cancel. Both parts are needed.
- Learn the five- and six-domain shapes in order of lone pairs added: trigonal bipyramidal → see-saw → T-shaped → linear, and octahedral → square pyramidal → square planar.

## Tips to remember

- **Balloons tied together.** Tie 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 balloons at their knots and they naturally push into linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral arrangements — exactly the VSEPR electron domain geometries.
- **Lone pairs are "invisible but bossy".** They aren't part of the shape's name, but they take up more room (repulsion: lone–lone > lone–bond > bond–bond) and squeeze the bond angles: 109.5° (CH₄) → 107° (NH₃) → 104.5° (H₂O).
- **Five domains: "lone pairs live around the waist."** Equatorial positions have only two neighbours at 90°, so lone pairs go there first. Adding lone pairs runs trigonal bipyramidal → see-saw → T-shaped → linear (XeF₂).
- **Six domains: "lone pairs sit opposite."** The second lone pair goes trans to the first, so octahedral → square pyramidal → square planar (XeF₄), never see-saw.
- **Polarity = polar bonds + shape that doesn't cancel.** Picture a tug-of-war: if equal teams pull from perfectly symmetric directions (CO₂, BF₃, CCl₄, SF₆, XeF₄), nothing moves and μ = 0. Swap one rope-puller for a different atom (CH₃Cl) and the molecule becomes polar.
- **Self-check routine:** Lewis structure → count domains (a multiple bond is one) → AXₘEₙ label → electron domain geometry → shape. If you remember one thing: NH₃ is *tetrahedral* in electron domains but *trigonal pyramidal* in shape.

## Key terms

- **VSEPR theory** — a model predicting molecular shape from the repulsion between electron domains around a central atom.
- **Electron domain** — a region of electron density around a central atom: a lone pair or a bond of any order.
- **Electron domain geometry** — the arrangement of all electron domains around the central atom.
- **Molecular geometry** — the arrangement of the atoms only; the shape of the molecule.
- **Axial position** — a position along the vertical axis of a trigonal bipyramid, at 90° to the equatorial positions.
- **Equatorial position** — one of three positions in the central plane of a trigonal bipyramid, 120° apart.
- **Bond dipole** — the separation of charge in a polar bond, shown as a vector from δ+ to δ−.
- **Dipole moment (μ)** — the product of separated charge and distance, μ = Q × r, measured in debye.
- **Polar molecule** — a molecule with a non-zero overall dipole moment.

## Summary

- VSEPR: electron domains around a central atom spread out to minimise repulsion; multiple bonds count as one domain.
- Repulsion order is lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair, so lone pairs shrink bond angles.
- Five domains give trigonal bipyramidal, see-saw, T-shaped and linear shapes; lone pairs go in equatorial positions.
- Six domains give octahedral, square pyramidal and square planar shapes; a second lone pair goes opposite the first.
- A molecule's dipole moment is the vector sum of its bond dipoles; symmetric shapes can be non-polar even with polar bonds.

questions.prompt: What is the molecular shape of ClF₃?
questions.explanation: Cl has 7 + 3(7) = 28 valence electrons in total; three Cl–F bonds plus F lone pairs use 24, leaving 2 lone pairs on Cl. That is 5 domains (AX₃E₂). Both lone pairs go equatorial, so the three F atoms form a T shape. Option A is tempting if you forget the lone pairs on Cl; option D is the shape for AX₄E.

questions.prompt: In a trigonal bipyramidal electron domain geometry, why do lone pairs occupy equatorial positions?

options.A: Equatorial positions are closer to the nucleus.
options.B: An equatorial position has only two neighbours at 90°, while an axial position has three, so placing lone pairs equatorially minimises the strongest repulsions.
options.C: Axial positions can only hold bonding pairs because they lie along the bond axis.
options.D: Equatorial positions are 180° from each other, so lone pairs are as far apart as possible.

questions.explanation: Repulsion is much stronger at 90° than at 120°. An axial site has three 90° neighbours and an equatorial site only two, so lone pairs, which repel most strongly, go equatorial. Option D is wrong because equatorial positions are 120° apart; the 180° pair is the two axial positions.

questions.prompt: Which of the following molecules is non-polar?
questions.explanation: XeF₄ is square planar (AX₄E₂): the four Xe–F bond dipoles point to the corners of a square and cancel, so μ = 0. SF₄ (see-saw), NF₃ (trigonal pyramidal) and BrF₅ (square pyramidal) all have shapes where the bond dipoles do not cancel. SF₄ is tempting because it also has four F atoms, but its lone pair makes the shape unsymmetrical.

questions.prompt: What are the electron domain geometry and the molecular shape of the ICl₄⁻ ion?
questions.explanation: Valence electrons: 7 + 4(7) + 1 = 36. Four I–Cl bonds and 12 Cl lone pairs use 32, leaving 4 electrons (2 lone pairs) on I. Six domains, AX₄E₂: octahedral domains, with the lone pairs opposite each other, giving square planar. Option A forgets the lone pairs on iodine; option C would need only one lone pair.

questions.prompt: Arrange the bond angles in CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O from largest to smallest.

options.D: All three are 109.5° because all have four electron domains.

questions.explanation: All three have tetrahedral electron domain geometry, but lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs and squeeze the bond angles: CH₄ (no lone pairs) 109.5°, NH₃ (one) 107°, H₂O (two) 104.5°. Option D is tempting because the domain count is the same, but it ignores the extra repulsion of lone pairs.

S in SO₂ has two bonding domains and one lone pair (AX₂E), so the electron domains are trigonal planar and the shape is bent (about 119°). The S–O bond dipoles do not cancel, so SO₂ is polar. Option A is the common trap: CO₂ is linear because carbon has no lone pair, but sulfur in SO₂ does.

questions.prompt: HF has a dipole moment of 1.82 D and a bond length of 92 pm. Estimate the partial charge on each atom as a fraction of the electron charge. (1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m; e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.explanation: μ = 1.82 × 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ = 6.07 × 10⁻³⁰ C m. Q = μ/r = 6.07 × 10⁻³⁰ / 9.2 × 10⁻¹¹ m = 6.60 × 10⁻²⁰ C. Fraction = 6.60 × 10⁻²⁰ / 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 0.41. Option D (0.04) comes from converting 92 pm to 9.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m instead of 9.2 × 10⁻¹¹ m; option B is the value for HCl.

questions.prompt: Which species has a molecular shape that is linear?
questions.explanation: Xe in XeF₂ has 2 bonding pairs and 3 lone pairs (AX₂E₃). The three lone pairs take the equatorial positions of a trigonal bipyramid, leaving the two F atoms axial at 180°. H₂S and OF₂ are bent (AX₂E₂), and SnCl₂ is bent (AX₂E). XeF₂ is a trap for students who assume lone pairs always make a molecule bent.
